outcomes.question: Our company has a September year-end. Its accounts for the year ended 30/09/2024 relate to YA 2025, and the tax return has been filed. Can we shred the supporting invoices on 01/10/2029?
outcomes.answer:
### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence verified for mapped issues; full request coverage unconfirmed.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for all listed issues.
**Individual applicability:** General guidance does not by itself establish eligibility or compliance in an individual case.
**Material evidence gaps:** None identified within the listed guidance. Full request coverage still requires an independent assessment.

#### IRAS — Corporate income tax

**Status:** Evidence verified

**IRAS company income-tax record retention and responsible person** (party in scope: Company)
- **IRAS rule explanation:** A company must retain source documents, accounting records and schedules, bank statements and other transaction-connected business records for at least five years from the relevant Year of Assessment (YA). IRAS gives examples: records for YA 2019 are retained to 31 December 2023, while records for YA 2023 are retained to 31 December 2027. For a company struck off and dissolved, the officer immediately before dissolution keeps the books and papers for at least five years after dissolution; for a wound-up company, the liquidator does so for at least five years from dissolution. Use the relevant YA for ordinary company tax records; the page’s examples distinguish December and non-December financial-year ends. After dissolution, the source identifies a different responsible person and starts the five-year period from dissolution. This is corporate income tax record guidance, not the separate GST record-retention rule. The ordinary YA period does not replace the separate dissolution-date duties for struck-off or wound-up companies. For case-specific application, consider: The relevant YA and financial-year period. Whether the company was struck off and dissolved or wound up, and its dissolution date. The source examples explain ordinary YA retention; they do not determine every record-specific retention requirement. A company-specific last-retention date requires the correct YA or dissolution date. For YA 2025, retain the records through at least 31 December 2029. The proposed disposal date 01/10/2029 is before the end of that period, so do not shred the records then. Filing the tax return does not end the retention period. [IRAS | Record Keeping Requirements](https://www.iras.gov.sg/taxes/corporate-income-tax/basics-of-corporate-income-tax/record-keeping-requirements)

- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports IRAS company income-tax record retention and responsible person): Your company must retain its records for at least 5 years from the relevant YA.

On this page:

Records That Your Company Must Keep

To run a business, it is important to have good record keeping.

• Make better business decisions

• Be aware of the financial status of your company (e.g. profit or loss position, whether there is internal fraud or theft)

• Reduce the cost and effort required to file the Corporate Income Tax Returns, and to reply to IRAS’ queries (if any)

Your company must retain its records (including source documents and bank statements) and be able to explain all transactions relating to its income, business expenses, and purchases. Your company must also keep its accounting records and schedules which summarise its business transactions in a systematic order.

Refer to the Record Keeping Checklist (PDF, 61KB) for a summary of the different types of records required.

For a more comprehensive guide on how to prepare and keep your company’s records, download the respective e-Tax Guides:

• For GST-Registered Companies: Record Keeping Guide for GST-Registered Businesses (PDF, 311KB)

• For Non GST-Registered Companies: Record Keeping Guide for Non GST-Registered Businesses (PDF, 264KB)

If your company qualifies to file Form C-S (Lite), download our Record Keeping Assistant (XLSX, 549KB) to help you to keep and organise your business records for tax preparation.

DOWNLOAD RECORD KEEPING ASSISTANT

Required Record Keeping Duration

Your company must retain its records for at least 5 years from the relevant YA.

Example 2: Companies with non-Dec financial year end

2023 | 1 Oct 2021 to 30 Sep 2022 | 31 Dec 2027

Wound Up Companies

Non-Compliance With Record Keeping Requirements

Q1. Can a company discard its records once it has completed its tax filing?

No, companies are required to retain its records for at least 5 years from the relevant YA.

Q2. Can a company keep its records manually in a physical form?

Companies are strongly encouraged to keep their records using an accounting software.

For source documents (e.g. receipts, invoices, vouchers), the company can keep them either in physical or electronic form.

Q3. Is record keeping only for the purposes of fulfilling statutory requirements?

Good record keeping practices not only enable a company to reduce the cost and effort required to file tax returns and reply to IRAS’ queries (if any), but also allow a company to make better business decisions and be more aware of its financial status.

Q4. Company X only keeps its bank statements as its records. Is this sufficient for record keeping purposes?

No, keeping only bank statements as records constitute poor record keeping and Company X may face penalties of up to $5,000.

Company X must ensure that it retains its source documents and is able to explain all transactions relating to its income, business expenses, and purchases. For example, source documents such as taxi receipts and travel documents must be retained to substantiate the company’s public transport or overseas travelling expense. Company X must also keep its accounting records and schedules which summarise its business transactions in a systematic order.

Q5.

There is no specific requirement for companies to migrate the accounting transactions recorded in the existing accounting software to the new accounting software.

However, after purchasing the new accounting software, a company must continue to retain and be able to retrieve the accounting transactions that had been recorded in the existing software for at least 5 years from the YA or end of the GST accounting period accordingly. Other business documents associated with these transactional records, such as source documents, accounting records and schedules and bank statements, should be retained as well.

#### IRAS — Corporate income tax

**IRAS company income-tax record retention and responsible person** (party in scope: Company)
- **IRAS rule explanation:** A company must retain source documents, accounting records and schedules, bank statements and other transaction-connected business records for at least five years from the relevant Year of Assessment (YA). IRAS gives examples: records for YA 2019 are retained to 31 December 2023, while records for YA 2023 are retained to 31 December 2027. For a company struck off and dissolved, the officer immediately before dissolution keeps the books and papers for at least five years after dissolution; for a wound-up company, the liquidator does so for at least five years from dissolution. Use the relevant YA for ordinary company tax records; the page’s examples distinguish December and non-December financial-year ends. After dissolution, the source identifies a different responsible person and starts the five-year period from dissolution. This is corporate income tax record guidance, not the separate GST record-retention rule. The ordinary YA period does not replace the separate dissolution-date duties for struck-off or wound-up companies. For case-specific application, consider: The relevant YA and financial-year period. Whether the company was struck off and dissolved or wound up, and its dissolution date. The source examples explain ordinary YA retention; they do not determine every record-specific retention requirement. A company-specific last-retention date requires the correct YA or dissolution date. The dissolution-based period runs for at least five years, through 15/08/2031. The relevant YA is also needed to compare the ordinary YA-based retention period before concluding when the records may safely be destroyed. On this page:

Records That Your Company Must Keep

To run a business, it is important to have good record keeping.

• Make better business decisions

• Be aware of the financial status of your company (e.g. profit or loss position, whether there is internal fraud or theft)

• Reduce the cost and effort required to file the Corporate Income Tax Returns, and to reply to IRAS’ queries (if any)

Your company must retain its records (including source documents and bank statements) and be able to explain all transactions relating to its income, business expenses, and purchases. Your company must also keep its accounting records and schedules which summarise its business transactions in a systematic order.

Refer to the Record Keeping Checklist (PDF, 61KB) for a summary of the different types of records required.

For a more comprehensive guide on how to prepare and keep your company’s records, download the respective e-Tax Guides:

• For GST-Registered Companies: Record Keeping Guide for GST-Registered Businesses (PDF, 311KB)

• For Non GST-Registered Companies: Record Keeping Guide for Non GST-Registered Businesses (PDF, 264KB)

If your company qualifies to file Form C-S (Lite), download our Record Keeping Assistant (XLSX, 549KB) to help you to keep and organise your business records for tax preparation.

Required Record Keeping Duration

Your company must retain its records for at least 5 years from the relevant YA.

Example 1: Companies with Dec financial year end

2023 | 1 Oct 2021 to 30 Sep 2022 | 31 Dec 2027

Watch our e-Learning video (from 09:50 to 10:55) for more examples on how long your company must keep its records.

&amp;amp;amp;amp;amp;nbsp;

Struck Off Companies

If your company has been struck off and dissolved, a person who was an officer of the company immediately before its dissolution must ensure that all books and papers of the company are retained for at least 5 years after the date on which the company was dissolved.

Wound Up Companies

If your company is being wound up, the liquidator of the company must ensure that all the books and papers of the company are retained for at least 5 years from the date of dissolution of the company.

Non-Compliance With Record Keeping Requirements

Q1. Can a company discard its records once it has completed its tax filing?

No, companies are required to retain its records for at least 5 years from the relevant YA.

Q2. Can a company keep its records manually in a physical form?

Companies are strongly encouraged to keep their records using an accounting software. Using an electronic record keeping system will incur lower manpower costs as the company would not have to manually track each and every business transaction. For source documents (e.g. receipts, invoices, vouchers), the company can keep them either in physical or electronic form.

Q3. Is record keeping only for the purposes of fulfilling statutory requirements?

Good record keeping practices not only enable a company to reduce the cost and effort required to file tax returns and reply to IRAS’ queries (if any), but also allow a company to make better business decisions and be more aware of its financial status.

Q4. Company X only keeps its bank statements as its records. Is this sufficient for record keeping purposes?

No, keeping only bank statements as records constitute poor record keeping and Company X may face penalties of up to $5,000.

Company X must ensure that it retains its source documents and is able to explain all transactions relating to its income, business expenses, and purchases. For example, source documents such as taxi receipts and travel documents must be retained to substantiate the company’s public transport or overseas travelling expense. Company X must also keep its accounting records and schedules which summarise its business transactions in a systematic order.

Q5.

There is no specific requirement for companies to migrate the accounting transactions recorded in the existing accounting software to the new accounting software.

However, after purchasing the new accounting software, a company must continue to retain and be able to retrieve the accounting transactions that had been recorded in the existing software for at least 5 years from the YA or end of the GST accounting period accordingly. Other business documents associated with these transactional records, such as source documents, accounting records and schedules and bank statements, should be retained as well.

outcomes.answer:
### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence verified for mapped issues; full request coverage unconfirmed.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for all listed issues.
**Individual applicability:** General guidance does not by itself establish eligibility or compliance in an individual case.
**Material evidence gaps:** None identified within the listed guidance. Full request coverage still requires an independent assessment.

#### CPF Board — CPF contributions

**Status:** Evidence verified

**CPF employer refund timing and application requirements** (party in scope: Employer)
- **CPF rule explanation:** Refund requests for CPF contributions generally must be made immediately and no later than one year from payment; the “PAYMENTS RECEIVED ON” field identifies the payment date. For conditional wages, the one-year period instead runs from when the wages are due to be repaid to the employer, as stated in employment terms or a mutual agreement, and that date must be entered in the application. Before applying, the employer must return the employee share directly to the employee. CPF Board effects refunds only to the extent of funds available in the employee’s CPF account. Excess Additional Wage ceiling contributions should be claimed promptly; excess CPF Annual Limit contributions paid from 2023 are automatically refunded to the employer’s Direct Debit Account from February 2024. The general and entire-submission application deadline is one year from contribution payment, using the “PAYMENTS RECEIVED ON” record field. Conditional-wage refunds use the repayment due date, not the contribution payment date. The employer must first return the employee share where applicable; refunds depend on funds available in employee CPF accounts. Excess Additional Wage ceiling contributions are a prompt-application category. CPF Annual Limit excess contributions paid from 2023 are refunded automatically to the employer from February 2024; this is distinct from an application for an AW-ceiling refund. For case-specific application, consider: Refund category and CPF payment date. For conditional wages, the contractual or mutually agreed repayment due date. Whether the employee share was returned and funds remain available in CPF account(s). For AW or annual-limit excess, the relevant year and excess category. Do not infer a refund deadline when the payment date, conditional-wage repayment date or calendar anniversary is unclear. The source does not establish that a particular refund application will be accepted or the amount CPF Board will refund. The payment record’s “PAYMENTS RECEIVED ON” date is 06/11/2025, making the one-year outer limit 06/11/2026; discovery of the error does not restart that period. [CPFB | Applying for refund of CPF contributions](https://www.cpf.gov.sg/employer/compliance-and-rectifications/applying-for-refund-of-cpf-contributions)

**Source:** CPFB | Applying for refund of CPF contributions (live external)
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports CPF employer refund timing and application requirements): Any request for refund of CPF contributions paid must be made immediately and no later than one year from the date of payment of the CPF contributions. You can refer to the “PAYMENTS RECEIVED ON” field in your record of payment to determine the date of payment.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports CPF employer refund timing and application requirements): Any request for refund of CPF contributions paid on conditional wages must be made immediately and no later than one year from the date wages are supposed to be repaid to the employer. This will be the date stated in the terms of employment or based on mutual agreement
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports CPF employer refund timing and application requirements): You’re responsible to refund the employee’s share of CPF contributions (where applicable) directly to your employee before submitting the application.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports CPF employer refund timing and application requirements): Refund is subject to availability of funds
We’ll effect the refund based on the available funds in the employee’s CPF account
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports CPF employer refund timing and application requirements): Refund of payments made in excess of Additional Wage ceiling
Once you have discovered that you paid CPF contributions in excess of the AW ceiling for any of your employees, you should apply for a refund of the CPF contributions made promptly.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports CPF employer refund timing and application requirements): Refund of contributions paid in excess of CPF Annual Limit
From February 2024, any CPF contributions paid in excess of the CPF Annual Limit will be refunded automatically to the employer's Direct Debit Account maintained with CPF Board. This applies to excess contributions paid from year 2023

Any request for refund of CPF contributions paid must be made immediately and no later than one year from the date of payment of the CPF contributions. You can refer to the “PAYMENTS RECEIVED ON” field in your record of payment to determine the date of payment.

Any request for refund of CPF contributions paid on conditional wages must be made immediately and no later than one year from the date wages are supposed to be repaid to the employer. This will be the date stated in the terms of employment or based on mutual agreement

You’re responsible to refund the employee’s share of CPF contributions (where applicable) directly to your employee before submitting the application.

Refund is subject to availability of funds
We’ll effect the refund based on the available funds in the employee’s CPF account

Refund of payments made in excess of Additional Wage ceiling
Once you have discovered that you paid CPF contributions in excess of the AW ceiling for any of your employees, you should apply for a refund of the CPF contributions made promptly.

Refund of contributions paid in excess of CPF Annual Limit
From February 2024, any CPF contributions paid in excess of the CPF Annual Limit will be refunded automatically to the employer's Direct Debit Account maintained with CPF Board. This applies to excess contributions paid from year 2023

#### CPF Board — CPF contributions

**Status:** Evidence verified

**CPF employer refund timing and application requirements** (party in scope: Employer)
- **CPF rule explanation:** Refund requests for CPF contributions generally must be made immediately and no later than one year from payment; the “PAYMENTS RECEIVED ON” field identifies the payment date. For conditional wages, the one-year period instead runs from when the wages are due to be repaid to the employer, as stated in employment terms or a mutual agreement, and that date must be entered in the application. Before applying, the employer must return the employee share directly to the employee. CPF Board effects refunds only to the extent of funds available in the employee’s CPF account. Excess Additional Wage ceiling contributions should be claimed promptly; excess CPF Annual Limit contributions paid from 2023 are automatically refunded to the employer’s Direct Debit Account from February 2024. The general and entire-submission application deadline is one year from contribution payment, using the “PAYMENTS RECEIVED ON” record field. Conditional-wage refunds use the repayment due date, not the contribution payment date. The employer must first return the employee share where applicable; refunds depend on funds available in employee CPF accounts. Excess Additional Wage ceiling contributions are a prompt-application category. CPF Annual Limit excess contributions paid from 2023 are refunded automatically to the employer from February 2024; this is distinct from an application for an AW-ceiling refund. For case-specific application, consider: Refund category and CPF payment date. For conditional wages, the contractual or mutually agreed repayment due date. Whether the employee share was returned and funds remain available in CPF account(s). For AW or annual-limit excess, the relevant year and excess category. Do not infer a refund deadline when the payment date, conditional-wage repayment date or calendar anniversary is unclear. The source does not establish that a particular refund application will be accepted or the amount CPF Board will refund. For the supplied conditional-wage repayment due date of 15/09/2026, the one-year outer limit is 15/09/2027. #### Ministry of Manpower — Employment requirements

**Status:** Evidence verified

**MOM itemised payslip issue and delivery requirements** (party in scope: Employer)
- **MOM rule explanation:** Employers must issue itemised pay slips to employees covered by the Employment Act together with payment. If that is not possible, the payslip must be given within three working days of payment. For termination or dismissal, the payslip must be given together with outstanding salary. MOM allows a soft or hard copy (including handwritten); a soft copy can be delivered electronically. The requirement applies to employees covered by the Employment Act. MOM permits soft or hard copy, including handwritten. The fallback is three working days after payment only when the employer cannot give it with payment. Items that do not apply need not be shown; MOM’s page gives overtime items as an example. This rule does not calculate final-salary deadlines or determine Employment Act coverage for a particular worker. For case-specific application, consider: Employment Act coverage. Payment date, whether a pay slip was provided with payment, and any termination/dismissal with outstanding salary. Three working days are not converted into calendar days. The captured page does not establish current coverage of a particular worker. [Itemised pay slips](https://www.mom.gov.sg/employment-practices/salary/itemised-payslips)

#### Ministry of Manpower — Employment requirements

**Status:** Evidence verified

**MOM itemised payslip issue and delivery requirements** (party in scope: Employer)
- **MOM rule explanation:** Employers must issue itemised pay slips to employees covered by the Employment Act together with payment. If that is not possible, the payslip must be given within three working days of payment. For termination or dismissal, the payslip must be given together with outstanding salary. MOM allows a soft or hard copy (including handwritten); a soft copy can be delivered electronically. The requirement applies to employees covered by the Employment Act. MOM permits soft or hard copy, including handwritten. The fallback is three working days after payment only when the employer cannot give it with payment. Items that do not apply need not be shown; MOM’s page gives overtime items as an example. This rule does not calculate final-salary deadlines or determine Employment Act coverage for a particular worker. For case-specific application, consider: Employment Act coverage. Payment date, whether a pay slip was provided with payment, and any termination/dismissal with outstanding salary. Three working days are not converted into calendar days. #### Monetary Authority of Singapore — Financial regulation

**Status:** Evidence verified

**MAS LFMC CEO and Director appointment approval** (party in scope: Company)
- **MAS rule explanation:** The current MAS LFMC Compliance Toolkit row 3 says an LFMC must seek prior MAS approval using Form 11 before appointing a Chief Executive Officer or Director, or before changing a Director’s appointment nature from Non-Executive to Executive; already being on the board does not remove approval for that change. Row 17 is a separate subsequent notification: it covers CEO or Director resignation, an Executive-to-Non-Executive change, changed CEO/Director particulars, and changed business interests or shareholdings provided in Form 11. Row 17 gives “As soon as practicable” for these notifications; its additional no-later-than-14-days limit is specifically attached to the resignation in item (i). The toolkit applies to Licensed Fund Management Companies and identifies the SFA and LCBR requirements in its scope. Row 3 calls for prior approval; row 17 separately concerns subsequent notifications and must not be substituted for row 3. Its 14-day time limit applies to item (i), resignation. This toolkit is not exhaustive and excludes requirements outside the SFA and fund-level requirements. The toolkit revision date is not a legal commencement date; this summary does not establish historic requirements. For case-specific application, consider: Whether the firm is an LFMC. Whether the person is a CEO or Director and whether the action is an initial appointment, Director nature change, resignation or later particulars change. General current toolkit guidance only; verify the applicable SFA provisions, licence conditions and current MAS requirements for a specific LFMC. Do not apply this row to VCFMs or other CMS licence holders without a source covering that regime. [LICENSED FUND MANAGEMENT COMPANIES](https://www.mas.gov.sg/-/media/mas-media-library/regulation/guidance/cmi/compliance-toolkits-for-fund-management-companies/sfa-compliance-toolkit-lfmcs29-may-2026-clean.pdf)

outcomes.question: At our LFMC, an existing non-executive director will take an executive role. Since he is already on the board, can we simply notify MAS afterwards? Would moving an executive director into a non-executive role follow the same process?
outcomes.answer:
### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence verified for mapped issues; full request coverage unconfirmed.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for all listed issues.
**Individual applicability:** General guidance does not by itself establish eligibility or compliance in an individual case.
**Material evidence gaps:** None identified within the listed guidance. Full request coverage still requires an independent assessment.

#### Monetary Authority of Singapore — Financial regulation

**Status:** Evidence verified

**MAS LFMC Director Executive and Non-Executive role changes** (party in scope: Company)
- **MAS rule explanation:** The current MAS LFMC Compliance Toolkit row 3 says an LFMC must seek prior MAS approval using Form 11 before appointing a Chief Executive Officer or Director, or before changing a Director’s appointment nature from Non-Executive to Executive; already being on the board does not remove approval for that change. Row 17 is a separate subsequent notification: it covers CEO or Director resignation, an Executive-to-Non-Executive change, changed CEO/Director particulars, and changed business interests or shareholdings provided in Form 11. Row 17 gives “As soon as practicable” for these notifications; its additional no-later-than-14-days limit is specifically attached to the resignation in item (i). The toolkit applies to Licensed Fund Management Companies and identifies the SFA and LCBR requirements in its scope. Row 3 calls for prior approval; row 17 separately concerns subsequent notifications and must not be substituted for row 3. Its 14-day time limit applies to item (i), resignation. This toolkit is not exhaustive and excludes requirements outside the SFA and fund-level requirements. The toolkit revision date is not a legal commencement date; this summary does not establish historic requirements. For case-specific application, consider: Whether the firm is an LFMC. Whether the person is a CEO or Director and whether the action is an initial appointment, Director nature change, resignation or later particulars change. General current toolkit guidance only; verify the applicable SFA provisions, licence conditions and current MAS requirements for a specific LFMC. Do not apply this row to VCFMs or other CMS licence holders without a source covering that regime.
